lookdev.gap: Replace the planet's nearest-filtered, unlit noise texture (stair-stepped coastlines, zero terrain relief, no cloud layer) that fills the lower third of every frame with a mip-mapped, sun-lit surface with shadowed relief, a drifting cloud sphere, and a proper Fresnel limb-scatter atmosphere.
lookdev.verdict: This is the best-looking piece of a competent indie: the sunset preset, the dawn nebula, the tracked-caps title typography and the banking camera all show real art direction, and there are no page errors on a clean run. But held next to a Star Fox Zero Corneria approach it falls apart on inspection: the planet is a pixelated, flat-lit texture, the lasers are soft bloom blobs instead of crisp bolts, Corneria Day washes to white with a clipped halo-less sun and smeared noise clouds, bloom eats the white hull into a smear, and every preset is the same frozen ring/wingman arrangement with a 'EXP 0.95 · BLOOM 0.40' debug caption that screams tech demo. A Nintendo AD would ship none of these frames yet. Also note a ~7s boot that caused a harness 'engine never booted' timeout under machine load on the first run.

ship.gap: The hull is a flat matte diffuse with no specular/environment reflection or ambient occlusion, so the white plating reads as painted cardboard instead of glossy Nintendo-grade armour — add a metallic/clearcoat response with a proper environment map and contact shadows between wings, pods and fuselage, and tame the sun bloom that wipes the whole ship to white in t010.
ship.verdict: Genuinely the strongest piece I've seen from this project: the Arwing silhouette, blue/white/red livery, orange G-diffuser glow, planet backdrop and confident lower-left typography all read as a real key-art layout, and the wings bank/flap responsively with zero console errors. Put beside a Star Fox Zero still, though, it loses on surface quality — no specular highlights, no AO, visibly aliased edges, a stubby boxy fuselage, slab-like wingtips and a black octagonal rear ring that looks like a tyre — and the t=10s frame is a bloom blow-out where the hull vanishes into white. Laser fire in the live test is a few tiny green dots in the distance, not crisp bolts. Competent-plus indie showcase, not yet something a Nintendo art director would ship.

flight.gap: Kill the milky low-contrast wash: give the ocean real shading (dark foreground values, wave normals, a hard specular sun-streak) and pull the bloom/fog down so the ship and mesas get true shadows and the water stops reading as a flat, horizontally-banded teal plane with a hard seam at the horizon.
flight.verdict: This is the strongest piece so far and genuinely competent indie-plus: a painterly sunset palette, blue/white Arwing with glowing G-diffusers, gold gates, a projected near/far reticle, clean HUD type, and clear boost/brake/roll states in the deterministic frames (t001 bank, t003 boost FOV kick + speed lines, t006 brake, t010 roll sparkle), zero console errors. But side-by-side with Star Fox 64 3D / Zero it loses on contrast and materiality: everything sits in the same pastel haze, the water is a flat banded plane with blob highlights and a visible seam against the low-poly mountains, the mesas are one repeated faceted mesh, the boost 'speed lines' are chunky white confetti shards that bury the ship, and the laser is a soft green smear rather than a crisp bolt. A Nintendo AD would recognise the intent instantly but would not ship the frame. Note: the stock shoot.mjs timed out on this piece under the current load-109 machine (~4 min per SwiftShader frame); frames were captured with an identical harness copy using a longer screenshot timeout, the realtime video was black except the last frame, so motion feel was judged from the deterministic t*.png only, and no interactive browser session was possible.

world.gap: Add real directional shadow-casting (spires, trees, towers onto the ground) plus a grass/soil detail texture and macro colour variation on the heightfield — right now every object floats on an unlit, perfectly uniform plastic-green lawn, which is the single thing that makes the frame read 'low-poly indie' instead of Nintendo.
world.verdict: Round 3 is genuinely the strongest world render so far: a confident saturated palette, a properly reflective river that mirrors the skyline and arches, red rock spires, a dense skyline with a glowing gateway arch, and a tasteful CORNERIA / SECTOR label; zero console errors. But side by side with Star Fox Zero's Corneria it still loses on a blind test: there is not a single cast shadow in any frame, the terrain is a flat-shaded textureless green blob with hard terraced stepping visible in t010, the city towers are grey boxes with tiled window sprites, and the clouds are soft billboards with no volume. It is a polished tech demo of a Corneria, not a first-party screenshot — competent-plus indie, not Nintendo.

enemies.gap: Thin the spawn density and stage the formations with depth and spacing so enemy silhouettes read individually instead of piling into an overlapping clump around the reticle — right now the frame is a cluttered mess of near-identical purple/green wedges with no clear hero target.
enemies.verdict: Genuinely strong art direction for a procedural piece: a sunset-over-ocean palette with a planet, Venomian dark-green/purple hulls with glowing amber and pink engine ports, laser bolts, lock-on markers, and confident HUD typography (VULTURE SQUADRON wave banner, sector label, score) that reads like a real game. But the composition is chaos — 20 hostiles stacked on top of each other with no spacing, silhouettes bleeding together, the player ship washed-out and center-clipped by enemies, and shading that is still flat toon-lit with faceted low-poly hulls that scream 'procedural'. Star Fox 64 3D / Zero would show 3-5 chunky, readable fighters in a clean V with clear depth. Only one frame captured before deadline, so motion, damage flash and death spin were not verified; competent indie plus, not first-party.

vfx.gap: The twin laser bolts — the headline effect — are nearly invisible thin pale streaks (t001, play1, play3); make them chunky, saturated green/cyan capsules with a hot white core, a long additive glow trail and a real muzzle flash so they read at any camera distance the way Star Fox 64/Zero bolts do.
vfx.verdict: The stage dressing (planet limb, magenta nebula, spaced-cap captions) gives this a confident first-party-ish composition, and the explosion stack is genuinely layered: shockwave ring, fireball, ember debris, smoke, plus a screen-filling smart-bomb sphere and a red lock-on reticle that feels correctly Star Fox. But side by side with a Star Fox 64 3D / Zero frame the actual effects are the weak link: lasers barely register, the shockwave is a thin flat 2D circle outline, the fireball reads as a cluster of five soft billboard puffs (t003), the smart bomb blows out to a featureless white disc that swallows the frame (t006), and the boost/afterburner shows raw cone geometry and jagged ribbon wedges (play1, play3 left edge). Competent indie with strong staging; a Nintendo art director would not ship these bolts or that ring. Note: video.webm frames were black for every piece in shots/, a harness capture issue, not a piece failure; errors.txt was clean.

hud.gap: Replace the generic Arial/Helvetica Bold-Italic system font with a bespoke condensed, rounded-corner display face (Star Fox Zero/64 3D style, with consistent tracking and a proper tabular numeral set) and shrink/shorten the mission banner so it no longer parks a 100px band over the Arwing and reticle for 3+ seconds.
hud.verdict: This is the most Nintendo-adjacent piece so far: the layered comm window with the procedural Peppy/Falco/Slippy portraits (mouth flaps confirmed between t003 and t014), the segmented glint shield bar, the boost→brake gauge recolour, the swept radar and the letter-drop GOOD LUCK / red WARNING banners are all readable, consistent and on-palette, with zero console errors. What stops it being a first-party frame is the typography — every label, number and dialogue line is plain Arial Bold Italic with letter-spacing, which screams CSS mock-up next to Star Fox's custom rounded face — and the banner composition, which sits exactly on the action horizon and occludes the ship, the reticle and the enemy wave. The portraits also read as flat vector clip-art rather than the shaded, lit character renders Nintendo would use, and the under-loaded backdrop (red hexagon placeholder enemies, no laser bolts) cheapens every screenshot. A Nintendo AD would ship none of these frames yet, but would recognise the layout as 80% there.

spacesim.gap: Fix the asteroid material: several rocks render as blown-out pure-white/cyan emissive blobs (t001, play3, t006) and every asteroid shares the same repeating leopard-spot Voronoi texture with flat decal craters — give them a proper dark rocky albedo, normal-mapped craters, varied per-instance hue/scale, and kill the over-bright ones.
spacesim.verdict: The Arwing itself, its glowing G-diffusers, the cloud-wrapped planet and the restrained cyan HUD (velocity/boost bars, radar, lock-on tags, U-TURN callout) are genuinely competent and the 6DOF camera roll produces some dramatic framings — no console errors, no default grey. But the belt betrays it: rocks are a single Voronoi 'cow-spot' texture scaled up, several are nuked to solid white, close-range drones read as untextured red/yellow boxes (t006), and near-camera clutter buries the ship in t001/play1 while t003 is 60% flat dark-brown polygon. A Nintendo art director would ship the Meteo frame with readable space, varied rock albedo and lit crater relief; this still says 'strong tech demo'. Note: video.webm was ~70% black frames due to the 2fps SwiftShader capture, not the piece.

onfoot.gap: Replace the boxy Roblox-style pilot (rectangular torso/limbs, flat sticker face with googly eyes glued onto a helmet) with a properly sculpted Fox McCloud silhouette — rounded muzzle and ears, tapered jacket/scarf, gloved hands actually holding a blaster, bent knees and elbows — because in a third-person piece the character occupies screen centre in every frame and currently single-handedly drops the image from 'Nintendo' to 'user-generated content'.
onfoot.verdict: The hangar itself is the best environment in this project: warm god-ray downlights against a cool navy shell, a legible 'GREAT FOX · HANGAR 01' signage lockup, holo-panels, a Corneria window, decal-stamped crates, cyan runway markers and a HUD with genuinely good tracking and hierarchy — no console errors, no default grey, no z-fighting. But the centre of every frame is a Minecraft/Roblox avatar: box torso, box shins, stump arms, a flat fox face pasted on a spherical helmet, and a stiff-legged 'run' with no lean, no arm swing amplitude and no squash on landing; the blaster bolts are tiny cyan pills and the training drones are anonymous dark cones. Beside Star Fox Zero's Great Fox interior or Fox in Adventures/Smash, a Nintendo art director would ship the set dressing and reject the hero on sight. Note: the realtime video came out black (SwiftShader at 1 fps under load ~100) so motion was judged from fixed-step frames; the two shoot.mjs runs also timed out at 30 s and I re-ran with a longer screenshot timeout — nothing else was changed.

boss.gap: The dreadnought reads as a clean but toy-like kitbash of blue cylinders and boxes with flat plastic shading — give the hull real material contrast (dark armour plates, panel-line grime, hot emissive vents, scale-selling greebles) so it feels like a kilometre-long capital ship instead of a hobby model floating in front of a wallpaper nebula.
boss.verdict: This is the most 'shippable' looking piece so far: the HUD typography (VENOMIAN DREADNOUGHT / GORGON, segmented phase bar, ROB 64 / Peppy comm panels) is genuinely first-party-grade, the magenta nebula plus lime planet palette is confident, and the targeted SHIELD GENERATOR reticle, red laser sweep telegraph and hit flashes read clearly. But the boss itself is the weak link: smooth uniform blue-grey plastic, unlit toy-cannon barrels, no sense of scale relative to the Arwing, and the bloom-blob explosions are small and muddy rather than screen-filling. Zero page errors, though the headless video came out black so phases 2–3 and the chain-reaction finale could not be verified from motion. Star Fox Zero's Andross-scale bosses still win on material richness and spectacle.

cinematics.gap: The piece takes >30s to boot under the harness (errors.txt: 'engine never booted', video.webm is 7.5s of pure black) and the intro has a visible clipping bug where the launching Arwing flies straight through the Great Fox's cannon barrel (p012.png) plus a stray floating blue cylinder in the hangar (t010.png) — fix boot cost and collision/path staging so the cinematic never shows geometry interpenetration.
cinematics.verdict: Genuinely the strongest-looking piece I've seen in this repo: the hangar launch (t010) with god-ray strip lights, cyan floor markings and Corneria framed in the bay door reads like a real first-party storyboard, the CORNERIA letterboxed title card and the MISSION COMPLETE tally panel have confident, well-kerned typography, and the Great Fox has actual material read and engine glow. But errors.txt records 'engine never booted' (automatic loss per brief), the recorded video is black for almost its whole length, the title-screen Arwing is a flat stock model dropped in front of a planet with no lighting integration, the Arwing intersects the Great Fox barrel mid-flyby, and a mystery blue cylinder floats in the hangar. Star Fox Zero/64 3D wins on polish and zero glitches; this is a very good indie cinematic, not a Nintendo ship.

audio.gap: Replace the boxy, flat-shaded placeholder Arwing (dark box wingtips, unlit G-diffusers, no contact shadow on the pad) with a properly sculpted, PBR-lit hero ship with glowing blue diffusers and a grounding shadow/reflection — it is the only element in an otherwise polished frame that screams 'tech demo'.
audio.verdict: This is the most cohesive piece I've judged in this repo: a real art-directed sound-test screen with a Corneria planet, hex launch pad, circular 3D spectrum ring, beat-synced stem lights, reactive Duck/SFX meters and confident HUD typography, with a convincing cyan→red palette shift between the main theme and battle loop, and zero errors. But the hero Arwing is a chunky low-poly box model with flat shading, dead G-diffusers and no shadow, the stem list collides with the planet limb, and the bars are plain bloomed boxes — a Nintendo art director would still ship their Corneria frame over this one. Strong competent-plus indie; not yet first-party.

playtest.summary: Full campaign completed end-to-end in one continuous run: title -> intro -> rail (Corneria, ~82s) -> GORGON boss -> all-range asteroid belt -> on-foot hangar -> mission-complete stats card -> back to title at 208s game-time, with zero page errors and zero console errors (shots/qa_play/report.json, shots/qa_play/*.png). Keyboard input verified live on :5173: Enter confirms the title, Enter skips the intro, WASD produces input.axes, Space registers fire; key handling is correct (single-tap misses seen only because SwiftShader frames span ~200ms — a sub-frame keyup artifact, not a game bug). Visuals are coherent and polished throughout: readable HUD with shield/bomb/radar/score, character com-boxes, boss health gauge and warnings, mission captions and objective text all legible with no HUD overlap; stage-entry screenshots that appear black are simply the 0.7s fade-in, confirmed by re-capturing 'complete' mid-stage (MISSION COMPLETE card renders correctly). Audio hooks are wired (music ducking, sfx calls on confirm/pause/fail) though muted during headless tests. Draw calls per stage: title 120 / intro 263 / rail 163 / boss 220 / space 192 / onfoot 340 / complete 423; triangles max ~211k — only 'complete' marginally exceeds the 400-call flag threshold. No soft-locks, crashes, or uncompletable objectives observed; campaign stage timeouts (240s boss, 180s space/onfoot) exist as safety nets but were never needed.
